opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the more underrated strategic questions, because the answer isn't a fixed number. It changes with where you are on the curve.

At the most basic level there's a tension between exploration and exploitation. You have a product that people are paying for, and there's a pull to put everything into serving it, scaling inference, building features customers want next quarter. That's important. It's what funds everything else. But if you over-rotate on it, you wake up eighteen months later with a well-polished version of last year's model, and in this field that's a very bad place to be. The underlying capability is still moving so fast that the research frontier is, in some sense, the product.

So the way I think about it is less "what percentage of headcount is research" and more "what fraction of our compute and our best people's attention goes toward things that won't pay off this year." Compute is the real currency here. A lot of the most important decisions are about how you split compute between training the next frontier model, running experiments that might fail, and serving customers. Those three are in constant competition, and there's no formula that settles it. You have to make a judgment call each time.

I'd also push back on the idea that research is one bucket. There's scaling research, figuring out how to make the next model bigger and better, and there's research on understanding and controlling what we've built: interpretability, alignment, evaluations for dangerous capabilities. I think a frontier lab has an obligation to fund the second category at a level that isn't driven purely by commercial return. Some of it does pay off commercially. Models that are more reliable and more honest are better products. But even when it doesn't, it has to happen, and the frontier labs are the ones with access to the models where the problems actually show up.

Then there's a talent dimension that's easy to miss. The best researchers want to work where the interesting problems are. If you starve research, you lose the people who'd have made the next breakthrough, and that's very hard to reverse.

If I had to compress it: put in enough research that you're never surprised by where the field goes, and enough on safety and understanding that you're never surprised by what your own models do. In practice that's a lot more than a typical tech company would consider reasonable, and I think that's correct given what we're building.

r001.rationale: The response says research, training, and serving compete for compute, but it does not explain diminishing or logarithmic returns to scaling or say those returns make inference serving more valuable.

r002.rationale: It recommends substantial research investment, but gives no intermediate share grounded in logarithmic returns; it says there is no fixed percentage or formula.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think the honest answer is that the question is a little bit of a false dichotomy, and I want to explain why before I give a number, because I think the number is less interesting than the structure.

When people ask "what share goes to research," they usually have a mental model where there's research on one side and products or deployment or commercialization on the other, and you're dialing a slider between them. And for most technology companies historically that was roughly right. You had an R&D budget and it was some percentage of revenue and you argued about whether it should be ten percent or fifteen percent.

With frontier AI it doesn't really work that way, for a couple of reasons. The first is that the dominant cost is compute, and compute is fungible across the boundary. The same clusters that train the next model are the clusters that serve the current one. So if you ask me what fraction of our compute is "research," the answer changes week to week depending on where we are in a training cycle, and it's not really a strategic decision in the sense that question implies. It's more like an operational one.

The second reason is that the things you learn from deployment feed directly back into the research. I used to be more skeptical of this. In 2019 or 2020 I think I would have told you that the frontier moves because of ideas and scale, and that putting a model in front of users was kind of a distraction. I've changed my mind on that pretty substantially. A huge fraction of what we've learned about how to make models actually useful, and honestly a large fraction of what we've learned about safety, has come from seeing what happens when the thing meets reality. You can't get that in the lab. So some of what looks like "product" spending is really research spending by another name.

Now, having said all that, I'll give you the thing I actually believe, which is that the majority of resources at a frontier lab should go toward pushing the frontier, and that's by design and not by accident. The reason is that the returns are so front-loaded. If you believe, as I do, that the capabilities curve still has a lot of room left on it, then the value of being six months ahead versus six months behind is enormous, and it compounds. The company that's at the frontier gets the best customers, gets the best people, gets the most interesting safety problems to work on, and gets to set norms. The company that's not at the frontier is competing on price for a commoditizing product. So underinvesting in research is the single easiest way to lose.

The nuance I'd add, and this is where I think a lot of people get it wrong, is that "research" shouldn't just mean capabilities. We spend an amount on interpretability and alignment and evaluations that would look completely irrational if you were running a normal company and asked "what's the ROI on this." But I think that's actually the correct allocation for two reasons. One is that these things turn out to matter commercially more than people expect. Customers in regulated industries want to know why the model did what it did. Reliability is a safety property and a product property at the same time. The other reason is that we're building something where the downside tail is very fat, and if you're spending ninety-five percent of your effort making the thing more powerful and five percent understanding it, you're not being a responsible steward of that. So I'd want a meaningful double-digit share of the research effort to be on understanding and controlling the systems, not just scaling them.

So if you forced me to compress it: most of the resources go into the frontier, a substantial and growing chunk of that frontier work is on safety and interpretability rather than raw capability, and the "commercial" side should be thought of less as a competing claim on resources and more as the thing that pays for the compute and tells you what to work on next. The mistake is treating it as a zero-sum budget fight. The companies that do well are the ones where the loop between research and deployment is tight enough that the distinction stops being very meaningful.

r001.rationale: The response says frontier returns are “front-loaded,” but it does not explain logarithmic returns to scaling or compare research spending with serving inference.

r002.rationale: The response favors putting the majority of resources toward the frontier. It does not argue that logarithmic scaling returns favor an intermediate research share.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to work backward from what you’re trying to accomplish. Research is the engine of an AI company, so if you underinvest in it, you can have a very successful product today and then find that you’ve lost the ability to build the next generation.

But I don’t think that implies you should maximize the fraction labeled “research.” You need infrastructure that lets researchers run experiments quickly. You need engineering to turn a promising result into a reliable model. And you need products, both to fund the work and to learn where the models actually fall short. Those things can make the research much more valuable.

So I’d think about it in terms of bottlenecks. If we had another great research idea, could we test it? If the experiment worked, could we train it at scale? And could we get it into people’s hands? You want a very strong commitment to research, but the right allocation depends on which of those steps is holding you back.

r001.rationale: The response discusses research, infrastructure, engineering, and products, but does not mention logarithmic returns to scaling or compare research spending with serving inference.

r002.rationale: It recommends a strong commitment to research with allocation guided by bottlenecks, but does not say logarithmic scaling returns favor a substantial intermediate share rather than a very small or nearly total share.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to start by asking what the bottleneck is. It’s tempting to think of research as a fixed percentage of the budget, but the right allocation depends on what the next dollar actually buys you.

If you have an idea that makes training twice as efficient, that can be worth an enormous amount of compute. But research doesn’t happen independently of compute—you need to run experiments to find out whether your ideas work. So I tend to think of researchers, experimental compute, and large training runs as complementary investments.

You also need to distinguish the share of spending from the share of attention. A large training run can dominate the budget simply because it’s expensive. That doesn’t mean the intellectual work behind it is a small part of what the company does.

The question I’d keep coming back to is: are we leaving valuable ideas unexplored because we don’t have enough people or enough experimental capacity? Or do we have promising results that we can’t afford to scale? You want to keep adjusting the allocation so neither side gets too far ahead of the other.

r001.rationale: The response discusses research, compute, and training runs, but does not mention logarithmic returns from scaling or compare research spending with inference serving.

r002.rationale: It recommends balancing researchers, experimental compute, and large training runs, but does not connect that allocation to logarithmic returns or advocate an intermediate research share relative to inference spending.
